title: Forgiveness, Ten Lepers, and the Coming Kingdom
summary: Jesus warns against causing others to stumble, commands repeated forgiveness, and tells his apostles that even small faith is enough and that servants do not earn thanks for doing their duty. On the road he heals ten men with leprosy, and only one, a Samaritan, returns to give thanks. Asked when the kingdom will come, he says it is already in their midst, then warns his disciples that the day of the Son of Man will arrive suddenly, as in the days of Noah and Lot.
story:
Jesus is still traveling toward Jerusalem, and Luke reminds the reader of it in verse 11, the second of three such markers in the central section (13:22, 17:11, 18:31). After the hard sayings about money in chapter 16, addressed partly to scoffing Pharisees, the teaching turns back to the disciples and to life inside their community: how they treat the vulnerable, how they forgive, how they think of their own service. The healing of the ten lepers then shows who actually responds to Jesus with gratitude, an outsider, echoing the Samaritan of the parable in chapter 10 and the Samaritan village that refused Jesus in chapter 9 (9:52-56).

The chapter ends by looking forward. The Pharisees ask when the kingdom will come; Jesus answers that it does not come by watching for signs and is already among them. Then he tells the disciples that the full revealing of the Son of Man still lies ahead and will come as suddenly as the flood and the fire on Sodom. That two-sided view of the kingdom, already present in Jesus and not yet complete, runs through the rest of Luke, and Jesus returns to the end in a longer discourse in Jerusalem (21:5-36). Chapter 18 follows directly with a parable about praying and not losing heart while the day delays.
historical:
Luke says Jesus was passing ‘through the middle of Samaria and Galilee’ (verse 11), which most translations render as along the border between them. The phrase is unusual, and some scholars take it as a sign that Luke's knowledge of Palestinian geography was loose, while others think he describes a route along the frontier running east toward the Jordan valley. The border was a real place of tension. Josephus tells how Galilean pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem for a festival were attacked and many killed at Ginae, a village on the boundary of Samaria and the great plain, in the governorship of Cumanus about AD 51, which led to Jewish reprisals and Roman intervention (Antiquities 20.118-136).

Samaritans lived in the central hill country around Shechem and Mount Gerizim. They traced their descent from the northern tribes of Israel, accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture (in their own form, the Samaritan Pentateuch), and worshiped at Gerizim rather than Jerusalem. The Judean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their temple on Gerizim in the late second century BC (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254-256), and hostility ran both ways: Josephus reports that under the governor Coponius (AD 6-9) some Samaritans scattered human bones in the Jerusalem temple courts at Passover to defile them (Antiquities 18.29-30). In this story a Samaritan is found among Jewish sufferers, since shared disease and exclusion could erase the usual boundaries.

The Law of Moses (Leviticus 13-14) gave priests the task of inspecting skin diseases, declaring a person unclean, and later confirming healing so that the person could return to worship and community, with offerings and a ritual of cleansing (Leviticus 14:1-32). The Hebrew tsara‘at and the Greek lepra, translated leprosy, covered a range of skin conditions (and could also affect cloth and walls), not only the disease now called Hansen's disease. Those afflicted had to tear their clothes, cover their lips, cry out ‘Unclean’, and live outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45-46), which is why the ten stand at a distance and shout. The Mishnah devotes a whole tractate (Nega‘im) to these laws, and a saying in the Babylonian Talmud counts the leper among those regarded as though dead (b. Nedarim 64b). By sending them to the priests before they were healed, Jesus asked them to act on his word. The ‘foreigner’ (allogenēs) of verse 18 is the word used on the stone inscriptions set up at the barrier of Herod's temple, forbidding any foreigner to pass into the inner courts on pain of death; one complete example was found in Jerusalem in 1871 and is in Istanbul, a fragment of another in 1935, and Josephus describes the warning (Jewish War 5.193-194, Antiquities 15.417).
cultural:
The ‘little ones’ of verse 2 are vulnerable members of the community, not only children. A millstone in Luke is literally a ‘stone of a mill’ (lithos mulikos), heavy enough to drown anyone; Mark and Matthew speak more vividly of a donkey's millstone, the upper stone of a large mill turned by an animal (Mark 9:42, Matthew 18:6). Rebuke of a brother or sister who sins is commanded in Leviticus 19:17 (‘you shall surely rebuke your neighbor’), and the Qumran community had rules for doing it properly (1QS 5:24-6:1). Jewish teachers debated the limits of forgiveness; a saying of Rabbi Yose bar Judah in the Babylonian Talmud (b. Yoma 86b), drawing on Amos's ‘for three transgressions and for four’, holds that God forgives a repeated sin three times but not a fourth. Jesus' ‘seven times in a day’ (verse 4) removes any such count, as does his ‘seventy-seven times’ in Matthew 18:21-22.

The mustard seed was proverbially tiny (13:19). The tree of verse 6 is the sukaminos, usually identified as the black mulberry, known for deep, spreading roots, which makes the picture of uprooting it by a word and planting it in the sea deliberately absurd; Luke uses a different word for the sycamore-fig Zacchaeus climbs (sukomorea, 19:4). Matthew and Mark have a mountain cast into the sea instead (Matthew 17:20, 21:21; Mark 11:23).

Slaves (douloi, BSB ‘servants’) were ordinary members of households in the Roman world, and a small farmer might own one who plowed, herded, and cooked. Jesus' picture in verses 7-10 assumes the expectations of his hearers: a master did not wait on the worker who came in from the field. He uses that shared assumption not to endorse slavery but to show disciples that obedience to God is owed, not a favor that puts God in their debt. Elsewhere Jesus overturns the same picture: the returning master who finds his slaves watching will dress himself to serve and have them recline at table (12:37), and Jesus says of himself, “But I am among you as one who serves” (22:27).

The examples of Noah and Lot drew on Genesis 6-7 and 19, and Jewish writers already paired the flood and Sodom as the great examples of sudden judgment on a careless world (Wisdom of Solomon 10:4-7, Sirach 16:7-8, 3 Maccabees 2:4-5; compare 2 Peter 2:5-7). The pillar of salt was a known landmark: the Wisdom of Solomon calls it a monument to an unbelieving soul (10:7), and Josephus claims to have seen it himself (Antiquities 1.203). Flat roofs served as living and sleeping space, reached by outside stairs, so someone on the roof could flee without going back inside. Grinding grain on a hand mill was daily women's work, often done by two women facing each other (compare Exodus 11:5). The bird of verse 37, aetos, can mean eagle or vulture; griffon vultures gathering over a carcass were a familiar sight (Job 39:27-30).
literary:
The chapter gathers several short units. Verses 1-10 are a cluster of sayings to the disciples on stumbling, forgiveness, faith, and duty, joined by the theme of life in the community. The apostles' request, ‘Increase our faith’, follows the command to forgive without limit, as if they felt the command was beyond them; Jesus answers that the issue is not the amount of faith but its object, then warns against thinking obedience earns a claim on God.

Verses 11-19 are a healing story with a twist. The lepers call Jesus epistatēs, ‘Master’, a title found only in Luke, where it is otherwise always on the lips of disciples (5:5, 8:24, 8:45, 9:33, 9:49). All ten are cleansed on the way, but the narrative turns on the one who ‘saw that he was healed’ and returned. Luke delays the key detail to the end of verse 16, ‘and he was a Samaritan’, and Jesus' three questions (verses 17-18) press it home. The pattern echoes the healing of Naaman the Syrian, who was cleansed by washing in the Jordan at Elisha's word and then returned to the prophet to confess the God of Israel (2 Kings 5:14-15). Jesus had cited Naaman in his first sermon as the one leper cleansed in Elisha's day (4:27). The verb ‘return’ (hupostrephō) is a favorite of Luke's, used 21 times in the Gospel and 11 in Acts, and nowhere else in the Gospels. The closing words, ‘your faith has made you well’, use the verb sōzō, which also means ‘saved’; all ten were cleansed, but to the one who returned Jesus speaks of faith and salvation (compare 7:50, 8:48, 18:42).

Verses 20-37 are a short discourse on the end, moving from a question by the Pharisees to teaching for the disciples. It is built on repeated warnings against ‘Look, here’ and ‘Look, there’ (verses 21 and 23), comparisons (lightning, Noah, Lot, Lot's wife), and pairs (two in a bed, two women grinding) that stress suddenness and separation. In the middle stands the necessity of suffering, ‘first He must’ (dei, verse 25), Luke's word for the divine plan (9:22, 24:7, 24:26). The saying about losing and preserving life (verse 33) repeats 9:24 in a new setting, and the discourse closes with a riddle-like proverb rather than a timetable.

outline.t: Unworthy servants who have only done their duty
Ten lepers healed; one Samaritan returns
The kingdom of God is in your midst
The day of the Son of Man, as in the days of Noah and Lot
Readiness and separation on that day

doctrines.note: Jesus ties forgiveness to repentance and removes any limit on it: “Even if he sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times returns to say, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive him” (verse 4). Rebuke and forgiveness belong together in the community of disciples, as honest confrontation and generous restoration.

The apostles ask for more faith; Jesus answers that its size is not the issue, since a mustard seed's worth is enough (verse 6). What matters is faith's object, the God who acts. The Samaritan shows faith that returns in gratitude and is told his faith has made him well (verse 19).

The kingdom does not come in ways that can be tracked by signs; in Jesus it is already present among his hearers (verses 20-21). Yet the day of the Son of Man still lies ahead and will come suddenly (verses 22-37). The chapter holds together a kingdom present now and a kingdom yet to be completed.

Jesus teaches that the Son of Man will be revealed publicly and unmistakably, like lightning across the sky (verse 24), after he has first suffered (verse 25), and that his coming will overtake a world absorbed in ordinary life, as the flood and the fire did (verses 26-30).

The healed Samaritan returns “praising God in a loud voice” and falls at Jesus' feet giving thanks (verses 15-16), and Jesus calls this giving glory to God (verse 18). Gratitude that turns back to its source is the heart of worship.

words.note: Skandalon, originally the trigger of a trap, then a snare or stumbling block, anything that causes someone to fall. It occurs 15 times in the New Testament, only here in Luke (verse 1), and the related verb skandalizō, ‘cause to stumble’, follows in verse 2. In the Septuagint it often translates words for a snare or obstacle (Leviticus 19:14). Paul calls the crucified Christ a skandalon to Jews (1 Corinthians 1:23). Here it is whatever leads a vulnerable believer into sin or away from faith.

Achreios, useless, unprofitable, and so ‘unworthy’. It occurs only twice in the New Testament: here (verse 10) and of the worthless slave who buried his talent (Matthew 25:30). In verse 10 it cannot mean that the servants did nothing useful, since they have done all they were commanded; it means they have no claim to reward. Some interpreters render it ‘mere servants’ or ‘servants to whom nothing is owed’.

Eucharisteō, to give thanks. It occurs 38 times in the New Testament, four in Luke: here (verse 16), in the Pharisee's prayer (18:11), and twice at the Last Supper (22:17, 22:19). It is frequent in Paul's letters, which open with thanksgiving. The Samaritan's thanks is the mark that separates him from the nine. The same word gave the Lord's Supper its later name, the Eucharist, the church's thanksgiving.

Allogenēs, foreigner, literally one of another race or stock. It occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 18). In the Septuagint it often translates the Hebrew for a foreigner excluded from holy things (Exodus 12:43, Leviticus 22:10). The same word appears on the temple inscriptions warning foreigners not to pass the barrier. Jesus names the Samaritan a foreigner and praises him as the only one who returned to give glory to God.

Sōzō, to save, rescue, heal, make whole. It occurs 106 times in the New Testament, 17 in Luke. The Gospels often use it of healing, and Luke's formula ‘your faith has saved you’ appears four times (7:50, 8:48, 17:19, 18:42), once of forgiveness and three times of healing. In verse 19 the healing is already done; what the returning Samaritan receives is a word about faith and wholeness that goes beyond cleansed skin. In verse 33 critical editions print a different verb, peripoieō (‘preserve’), where later manuscripts have sōzō.

Paratērēsis, observation, occurs only here in the New Testament (verse 20). In Greek writers it could describe close watching for signs, such as a physician observing symptoms or an astronomer observing the heavens. Jesus says the kingdom does not come ‘with observation’, meaning that it cannot be calculated or pinpointed by watching for signs, a warning against the apocalyptic reckonings of his day and ours.

Entos, inside, within. It occurs twice in the New Testament: here (verse 21) and in Matthew 23:26, ‘the inside of the cup’. With a plural pronoun, entos humōn can mean ‘within you’ (inside each person), and older translations, following the Latin intra vos, render it so. Many modern versions render it ‘among you’ or ‘in your midst’, pointing to Jesus' own presence, and C. H. Roberts (1948) proposed ‘within your reach’ from the papyri. See the first hard question below.

Paralambanō, to take, take along, receive. It occurs 49 times in the New Testament, six in Luke. In verses 34-35 one ‘will be taken’ (paralēmphthēsetai) and the other ‘left’ (aphethēsetai). The verb often means to take someone into one's company (Matthew 1:20, 17:1; John 14:3, where Jesus will ‘take you to Myself’), a point used by those who see the one taken as rescued. Others reply that context, not the verb alone, decides, and the flood ‘took’ its victims (Matthew 24:39, a different verb).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus doing what belongs to God and receiving what belongs to God. The Samaritan returns praising God and falls at Jesus' feet, and Jesus treats the return to him as giving glory to God (verses 15-18). In the story of Naaman, the healed foreigner returned to the prophet Elisha but gave the glory to the God of Israel alone (2 Kings 5:15); here the healed foreigner's thanksgiving is directed to Jesus himself, and Jesus accepts it. Luke has already called Jesus a prophet greater than Elisha (7:16, 4:27), and here the one who cleanses lepers with a word is more than a prophet.

Jesus also names himself the Son of Man, a title drawn from Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and receives an everlasting dominion. The day of the Son of Man in this chapter is that coming, public and unmistakable like lightning (verse 24). Yet in verse 25 Jesus insists that first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation. Glory comes by way of the cross, the pattern of all three passion predictions (9:22, 9:44, 18:31-33) and of the risen Christ's own explanation: “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (24:26).

The kingdom that is ‘in your midst’ (verse 21) is present because the king is present. In Jesus' healings and forgiveness God's reign is already breaking in (11:20), and his warnings about the day to come show that it will be completed only when he is revealed. The healing of the Samaritan also anticipates the mission to Samaria in Acts, where Philip preaches Christ in a Samaritan city and there is great joy (Acts 8:4-8), and Jesus' commission to be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The church confesses him as the one who will come again to judge the living and the dead, and this chapter is one of the texts on which that confession rests.
interpretation:
The saying about the kingdom ‘within you’ (verse 21) has had a long life of its own. Origen (On Prayer 25) read it as the reign of God within the soul of the saint, which grows until God is all in all, and Athanasius's Life of Antony (chapter 20) has Antony tell his monks that virtue needs no long travel, because the kingdom of God is within them. The Gospel of Thomas (sayings 3 and 113) has sayings in which the kingdom is inside and outside the disciples, or spread out upon the earth unseen. The Latin intra vos, Luther's inwendig in euch, and the King James ‘within you’ carried the inward reading into the modern church. Leo Tolstoy took the phrase as the title of his manifesto of Christian nonviolence, The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894), which Mohandas Gandhi said overwhelmed him when he read it in South Africa. Modern commentators have mostly preferred ‘among you’ or ‘in your midst’, noting that Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and that the kingdom in Luke is present in Jesus' person and works, and C. H. Roberts (The Kingdom of Heaven (Lk. XVII.21), Harvard Theological Review 41, 1948) argued from the papyri for ‘within your reach’ or ‘in your power’. English Bibles are divided accordingly.

The ten lepers were read allegorically by the fathers and medieval preachers: Augustine (Questions on the Gospels 2.40), followed by Bede, took leprosy, with its blotches of mixed color, as a figure of false teaching that mixes truth and error, and the cleansing as coming to true doctrine in the church; the nine who did not return showed that right belief without gratitude is incomplete, and the Samaritan's return became a type of the Gentile church's thanksgiving. The Reformers drew the lesson of thankfulness and the sufficiency of Christ's word. In Lutheran Leipzig verses 11-19 were the Gospel for the Fourteenth Sunday after Trinity, and Bach wrote Es ist nichts Gesundes an meinem Leibe (BWV 25, 1723), Jesu, der du meine Seele (BWV 78, 1724), and Wer Dank opfert, der preiset mich (BWV 17, 1726) for it. The Orthodox read the story on the Twelfth Sunday of Luke; the Revised Common Lectionary and the Roman lectionary read verses 11-19 in October of Year C, and the Revised Common Lectionary also appoints it for Thanksgiving Day in Year A.

Verse 10 figured in the medieval and Reformation debates about merit. Protestant readers cited it against any claim to deserve reward from God; Catholic theology replied with Augustine's principle (Letter 194) that when God rewards human merits he crowns his own gifts, a reading that also takes the verse as ruling out any claim made in pride.

The sayings about one taken and one left (verses 34-35, with Matthew 24:40-41) became central to the doctrine of a secret rapture developed by John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren in the 1830s and spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909). In twentieth-century American popular culture they inspired Larry Norman's song I Wish We'd All Been Ready (1969), the film A Thief in the Night (1972), and the Left Behind novels by Tim LaHaye and Jerry B. Jenkins (from 1995). Many commentators, including some dispensationalists such as John MacArthur, read the one ‘taken’ as taken in judgment, as in the days of Noah.
text:
Three differences between manuscripts affect English Bibles. Verse 36, ‘Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other left’, is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts, including P75, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, and from most later Greek manuscripts as well. It appears in Codex Bezae, some minuscules (family 13), and some Latin and Syriac witnesses, and it entered the printed Textus Receptus and so the King James Version. Bruce Metzger explains the committee's judgment that copyists added it from Matthew 24:40, while granting that an accidental omission is possible. Modern versions omit it or place it in a note, so the numbering skips from 35 to 37, as the BSB shows.

In verse 24 the words ‘in His day’ are absent from P75, Vaticanus, and Bezae, and editors print them in brackets; the sense is unaffected. In verse 9 the King James Version adds the reply ‘I trow not’ (I think not), from later manuscripts that the earliest copies lack. Verse 21 has no manuscript problem, but the translation of entos humōn varies: ‘within you’ (King James Version, older NIV), ‘in the midst of you’ (RSV, ESV), ‘among you’ (NRSV, current NIV), and the BSB's “in your midst”.

teach.big: Disciples live between a kingdom already present in Jesus and a day of the Son of Man still to come, and they show it by guarding the weak, forgiving without limit, serving without claiming reward, and returning to give thanks.

outline.t: Causing a vulnerable believer to fall is a grave sin, and Jesus warns his own followers first.
Honest rebuke and unlimited forgiveness belong together in the community of disciples.
Faith's power lies in its object, God, not in its size; a little is enough.
Obedience is owed to God, not a favor that makes him our debtor.
Jesus hears the cry of the excluded and asks them to act on his word before they see the result.
All ten were cleansed, but only the grateful outsider returned, and to him Jesus speaks of faith and wholeness.
The kingdom is not calculated by signs; it is already present in Jesus among his hearers.
The Son of Man's coming will be public and unmistakable, but the cross comes first.
Judgment overtakes a world absorbed in ordinary life, as in the days of Noah and Lot.
Readiness means not clinging to possessions or looking back; that day will divide people who seemed alike.

teach.pitfalls:
Verses 3-4 are sometimes taught as if forgiveness meant pretending nothing happened, restoring trust immediately, or never naming wrong. Jesus commands rebuke first and ties forgiveness to repentance; forgiveness releases the debt and the desire for revenge, but it does not require returning to danger or dropping accountability. Verses 5-6 are misused to teach that enough faith guarantees any outcome one names, as in prosperity teaching; Jesus' point is that faith's power lies in God, not in the believer's technique. Verses 7-10 should not be read as approving slavery or as picturing God as a cold master; Jesus overturns that picture elsewhere (12:37, 22:27).

The ten lepers should not be reduced to a lesson in manners. The story turns on an outsider who recognizes where God is at work and returns to Jesus, and on the salvation spoken to him. On verse 21, do not preach ‘the kingdom within you’ as if the kingdom were only an inner spiritual state or human potential; that reading must reckon with the rest of the chapter, where the kingdom's completion is a public event. Equally, do not dismiss the inward reading's truth that God reigns in the hearts of his people. On verses 34-35, present the rapture reading and the judgment reading fairly; this is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ, and the passage's own emphasis is suddenness and readiness, not a timetable. Avoid setting dates or reading current events as the signs Jesus says will not be given (verses 20-23).
teach.pastoral: The command to forgive seven times in a day will press on people who have been abused, betrayed, or repeatedly harmed, and on those who feel guilty that they cannot yet forgive. Teach it with care: Jesus speaks of a brother who sins and repents, and the first command is to rebuke. Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation, trust, or silence, and it never requires someone to stay in an abusive relationship or to keep a crime secret; safety and, where needed, reporting to the authorities come first. Many find forgiveness is a road walked over time rather than a single act. The story of the lepers may press on people with chronic illness, disability, or conditions that isolate them; the text shows Jesus hearing those who stand at a distance, and it should not be used to suggest that those not healed lack faith. Teaching on the end can frighten anxious listeners or children; the passage calls for readiness and trust in the Son of Man who first suffered for his people, not for fear.

hard.q: Is the kingdom of God ‘within you’ or ‘among you’?
hard.a:
The inward reading has strong defenders. Grammatically, entos most naturally means ‘inside’, as it does in its only other New Testament use (Matthew 23:26), and Greek had other words for ‘among’ (en mesō, as in 22:27). Origen, Athanasius, and much of the church's tradition of spiritual writing read the verse as God's reign in the soul; the Latin Vulgate, Luther, and the King James Version translate it so; and Leo Tolstoy (1894) built his reading of Christianity on it, as have many modern spiritual teachers outside the church who take it to mean a divine spark in every person. The Gospel of Thomas shows that an inward reading circulated early. Defenders of this reading argue that ‘among you’ is a modern theological preference, not a demand of the Greek.

The other side replies from context. Jesus is answering Pharisees who had opposed him, and he is unlikely to tell them that the kingdom is inside them; the contrast with ‘Look, here it is’ suggests location rather than interiority; and in Luke the kingdom is present in Jesus' person and works (11:20). Papyri show entos with a plural pronoun meaning ‘in the midst of’ or ‘within the domain of’, and C. H. Roberts (1948) argued for ‘within your reach’. Most modern commentators prefer ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’, and most modern translations (RSV, ESV, NRSV, NASB, current NIV) follow. Some combine the two: the kingdom is present in Jesus among them and is received inwardly by faith. Both readings are defended by serious scholars, and the translation choice should be made with its reasons stated, not as a test of orthodoxy. What neither reading allows is a kingdom that can be tracked by signs, or a kingdom that is merely human potential without the king who brings it.

hard.q: What does it mean that one will be taken and the other left, and is this about a rapture?
hard.a:
The rapture reading is held by many dispensational premillennialists, following John Nelson Darby in the 1830s and later the Scofield Reference Bible, and it is widely assumed in American evangelical culture through the Left Behind novels. On this view, the one ‘taken’ is a believer gathered to Christ, as in 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, and the one ‘left’ remains for judgment. Its defenders note that paralambanō often means to take someone into one's company, as when Jesus promises to take his disciples to himself (John 14:3). Skeptical critics raise a different objection: that these sayings expected the end within Jesus' own generation and that the church has had to reinterpret them since.

Other interpreters, including many who are premillennial, read the one taken as swept away in judgment. In the examples Jesus has just given, judgment ‘destroyed them all’ while Noah and Lot were spared (verses 27 and 29); in Matthew's parallel the flood ‘swept them all away’ (Matthew 24:39); and when the disciples ask where, Jesus answers with vultures gathering over a carcass (verse 37), an image of death. John MacArthur, himself a dispensationalist, takes this view of the passage, and Darrell Bock notes the several options while stressing that the separation will be obvious and final. On the question of timing, Christians respond that Jesus explicitly refused to give signs or dates (verses 20-23; Acts 1:7). On either reading, Jesus' point is the same: the day will come without warning, it will divide people who seemed to share the same life, and readiness cannot be borrowed from the person beside you. How these sayings fit a wider sequence of the end is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ.

observe: What does Jesus tell the disciples to do when a brother sins, and in what order (verses 3-4)?
What do the ten lepers call Jesus, and what does he tell them to do before they are healed?
What were people doing in the days of Noah and Lot when judgment came (verses 27-28)?
interpret: Why might the apostles have asked for more faith right after the command to forgive without limit?
All ten were cleansed. What did the Samaritan receive that the nine did not, and why?
How can the kingdom be already in your midst (verse 21) and still be coming in a day that has not yet arrived (verses 22-30)?
apply: Where is repeated forgiveness hardest for you, and how is forgiving different from trusting again?
Nine were healed and did not come back. What gifts have you received that you have never returned to thank God for?
The people of Noah's and Lot's day were eating, marrying, and building. How can ordinary, good things absorb us so fully that we stop watching?
